items.rationale: The difference is who owns the control flow: in a workflow, code written in advance sets the steps and their order; in an agent, the model decides the next step and when to stop. Model size (a), whether a model is called at all (c), and how many models are used (d) do not separate the two.

Only option c has code fixing the sequence (lookup, one model call, send) the same way for every request. In a, b and d the model chooses the tools, their order or how many calls to make, which is the agent pattern.

The 30 fixed-step bookings suit a workflow: 30 x 2 = 60 calls. The 10 open-ended requests suit an agent: 10 x 5 = 50 calls. Total: 60 + 50 = 110 model calls per day. Answering 200 (all 40 as agents) or 80 (all 40 as workflows) ignores matching each design to its kind of request.

When the steps and their order are known in advance and the same every time, a fixed workflow is the better choice: fewer model calls, predictable cost and behaviour, and easy testing. Flexibility is not free (b), an agent does not save calls here (c), and a workflow does not adapt to unplanned requests by itself (d).

The needed steps depend on what each result shows, so they cannot be fixed beforehand; that is where an agent's flexibility is worth its extra cost. A workflow chosen for being cheap (a) or for a set sequence (b) would force the wrong steps on the task, and merely writing the final answer (d) does not make a system an agent.

This is a routing workflow: the model makes one bounded choice among paths the team built, and code runs the fixed steps of each. The model does not choose steps, order or when to stop, so the code still owns the control flow. Using a model (c) or influencing which path runs (b) does not make a system an agent, and the design is not 'neither' (d): it is a workflow.
